interactions.summary: A student says medieval scholars are too material and ulteriorly motivated, another student extends the point with a Crusader Kings analogy about theology being used to justify territorial power, and Jiang agrees while saying the same pathology still exists today.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Students interpret Dante with Jiang agreement

interactions.summary: Carol continues reading Paradise 11, shifting from Dante's critique of earthly studies into Thomas Aquinas's speech from within heaven's radiance.

Jiang explains the canto's unusual structure: Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican, will praise Francis and criticize his own order, Bonaventure will later mirror the move for the Franciscans, and Aquinas's opening references 'they fatten well' as a diagnosis of Catholic corruption.

speaker_notes.note: The speaker appears to be the same student who has been pressing Jiang with comparative and methodological objections; the tone is argumentative but supportive of the basic reading here.

claims.claim: Jiang agrees with the students that Dante's complaint is about theology and academic study being pursued for power, status, and material advantage rather than for God and truth.
He says the corruption Dante criticizes in medieval theology and scholarship is not fundamentally different from the condition of academia today.

Jiang says the paradox of the canto is that Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican, praises the Franciscans and criticizes his own order, while Bonaventure will later do the reverse for the Dominicans and Franciscans.
claims.temporal_scope: Structural reading of the canto stated on 2026-06-17.

claims.claim: He interprets Aquinas's phrase 'they fatten well' as a shorthand diagnosis of corruption inside the Catholic Church.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang collapses medieval theology and current academia into the same corruption pattern: learning used to amass power.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Quite honestly, it's no different today
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It pulls Dante out of the medieval past and turns the canto into a live diagnosis of present institutions.

signature_moments.moment: Each order can only be judged truthfully when its rival praises it and it criticizes itself.
signature_moments.source_phrase: he will criticize his own order
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This gives the packet a memorable model of cross-order moral testimony rather than self-congratulation.

signature_moments.moment: Aquinas's compressed phrase about fattening is unpacked into an image of ecclesial overgrowth and corruption.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is one of the first sharp verbal hooks Jiang gives the class for the canto's institutional critique.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's shorthand for Aquinas's criticism of institutional corruption inside the Church, especially orders that have grown materially bloated or morally compromised.
The kind of intellectual maneuvering Jiang associates here with using the mind instrumentally for power rather than spiritually for truth.

chronology_notes.note: On 2026-06-17 Jiang explicitly bridges Dante's medieval critique to present-day academia before moving deeper into Aquinas's account of Church corruption.

uncertainty_notes.note: The Crusader Kings example is a student's modern analogy for theologized power rather than evidence Jiang himself introduces from the historical text.
